title: A Less-Is-More Strategy for America
gist: Barry Posen argues the U.S. military, built for short, sharp great-power wars, is worn out by the Iran war and constant deployments; instead of a bigger and costlier force, Washington should scale back commitments, adopt an activity budget and hand more of Europe's defense to Europeans.

insights.claim: The USS Abraham Lincoln strike group returned October 8 after 320 days at sea, a near record, with supply shortages, plumbing and water-contamination problems, falling morale and eight attempted suicides.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of readiness strain from the Iran war deployment.
insights.locator: On October 8, the USS Abraham Lincoln

insights.claim: The U.S. military is not built for the near-constant use of recent decades: since the Cold War it has been sized to win two major conflicts quickly, so it lacks units, weapons and personnel for never-ending conflicts.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Structural mismatch between force design and actual use explains stockpile and readiness problems.
insights.locator: These problems all share the same root cause

insights.claim: The F-35 'full mission capable rate' has deteriorated from 38 percent to 25 percent since 2021, and overall air force aircraft readiness has also declined, partly from overwork.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Readiness decline in the flagship platform undercuts the case that buying fancier hardware fixes the problem.
insights.locator: In the air force, the F-35's

insights.claim: Deferred maintenance creates cascading repair delays: a ship staying longer in dry dock forces others to wait, leaving the navy with fewer ready combat ships; army vehicles reach depots in unexpectedly poor condition; and since 2024 navy warships have repeatedly gone to sea undercrewed.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Maintenance backlogs compound, which supports demand for ship repair and depot capacity.
insights.locator: The result is a worn-down military

insights.claim: U.S. nonnuclear forces, consuming more than 80 percent of the defense budget, are designed for a clash with China, Russia or both, emphasizing precise, long-range, stealthy weapons that are not suited to mass production.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: The force favors exquisite systems over volume, a constraint in prolonged wars.
insights.locator: The U.S. nonnuclear forces, which consume more than 80 percent

insights.claim: At about $100 million each the F-35 is not designed for mass production, nor are the long-range stand-off missiles preferred in the opening of a great-power war.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Production-scale limits in high-end munitions point to supply bottlenecks for defense primes.
insights.locator: At $100 million each, the F-35 fighter aircraft

insights.claim: U.S. theater ballistic missile defenses are meant to protect U.S. forces and essential military infrastructure, and using them to defend cities quickly exhausts the missile supply.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Interceptor consumption in regional wars depletes scarce stocks needed for a great-power fight.
insights.locator: The U.S. military has developed sophisticated theater ballistic missile defenses

insights.claim: Adversaries have adapted: rather than building weaker copies of great-power militaries, they prepare to take a beating and keep fighting, which is why the U.S. could not rapidly overpower Iran as it did Iraq in 1990-91.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Wars with middle powers can become attritional, raising munitions and duration risk.
insights.locator: But Washington's enemies have smartened up

insights.claim: Casualty-averse politicians spend high-end weapons stockpiled for great-power wars on regional conflicts and deploy scarce air defenses to protect allies' cities so allies do not look for new partners or compromise with enemies.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Political incentives drain strategic reserves, increasing replenishment demand.
insights.locator: Because the American people hesitate to support wars abroad

insights.claim: U.S. policymakers overuse the military because they no longer believe in diplomacy, and commanders usually salute and say yes when asked to act.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Suggests continued high operational tempo regardless of administration.
insights.locator: U.S. policymakers also generally overuse the military

insights.claim: Congress appears poised to raise the Pentagon base budget by over 25 percent to $1.1 trillion for fiscal 2027, with officials seeking another $350 billion above base in a later bill.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: A very large defense budget step-up supports defense-industry demand, though Posen argues it will not fix readiness.

insights.claim: Defense officials want to add over 40,000 service members, only about a 3 percent increase, too small to fill the units needed to fix readiness, while larger recruiting would require higher wages that raise personnel's share of the budget; conscription would cause backlash.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Personnel costs are a binding constraint that can crowd out procurement.
insights.locator: Defense officials also want to add over 40,000 new service members

insights.claim: The defense industrial base is barely keeping up with current demand, so fancier weapons cannot overcome the strain of constant deployments and repeated wars.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Capacity constraints limit how quickly new money converts to capability.
insights.locator: The defense industrial base is barely keeping up

insights.claim: Posen proposes an 'activity budget', set by the Pentagon at Congress's direction and published alongside the dollar budget, that caps flying hours, ship days at sea and field training days at levels the force can sustain without damaging readiness.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: A public activity cap would constrain deployments and is a policy to watch for operational-tempo reform.
insights.quote: Washington should cut its policy coat to fit the available cloth.
insights.locator: The activity budget should not be classified

insights.claim: The U.S. Navy already knows the activity level its fleet can support, set out in its Optimized Fleet Response Plan, but presidents and defense secretaries have ignored it whenever they wanted to deploy more forces.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Existing planning limits are routinely overridden, so reform requires political accountability.
insights.locator: The U.S. Navy already knows the activity level

insights.claim: Washington should hand more of Europe's defense to Europeans: principal European states have ample resources to deal with Russia, NATO's supreme allied commander should be a European, and many of the tens of thousands of U.S. troops in Europe should come home.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Points toward reduced U.S. force posture in Europe and higher European defense spending.
insights.locator: To help lighten its load, Washington will need to hand off

insights.claim: The United States is inherently very secure, being rich, resource-endowed, ocean-insulated and surrounded by weak neighbors, so only huge shifts in the balance of power in Asia, Europe or the Middle East could seriously affect it.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: A restraint thesis against the consensus that the U.S. must police everywhere.

insights.claim: Grand-strategy restraint might allow cuts to the defense budget, which Posen says the Pentagon may need to contribute to if concerns about ballooning U.S. deficits are correct.
insights.speaker: Barry R. Posen
insights.so_what: Links defense spending to fiscal sustainability, a long-run risk to the defense-spending upcycle.
